The etymological information seems questionable.  ''Artefact'' appears to have first seen light in English around 1820 from Latin by way of Italian.  Sir Julian Huxley wasn't born until 1887.  Confirm? [[User:E. abu Filumena|E. abu Filumena]] 06:39, 16 Feb 2005 (UTC)

== Removed quote from sense 4 ==

I have removed the quote from sense 4, because Philip Weiss says the quote is not actually from him, he was quoting someone else who was quoting someone else yet. When I search for it in books.google.com it shows up only once, in "Men Confront Pornography" By Michael S. Kimmel, but the content of that book is not available for viewing, so I can't verify who it came from. Furthermore Philip Weiss disagrees with quote, so it's not fair to make it appear that it came from him. - [[User:Doug Hockin|dougher]] 00:05, 20 February 2009 (UTC)

'artefact' is the spelling in the Cambridge dictionary with 'artifact' as US; Chambers has both spellings together.
I think this is true of most UK English dictionaries.
Once again OED is the odd one out, as it is with 'ize' instead of 'ise'.
mike Nelson

== military maneuver ==

Am I dreaming or is there a military sense (or usually military sense) of a movement made on a battlefield. Not the same as the current military sense, which is in the plural, [[maneuvers]], training exercises. == [[WT:FEED]] == {{archive-top|WT:FEED}} == [[:apologize]] == Apologize is an alternate form of Apologise. Not the other way around. :They're alternative forms of each other. Neither is more correct than the other, though the spelling with ''z'' is closer to the Greek original {{m|grc|ἀπολογίζομαι}}. —[[User:Angr|Aɴɢʀ]] ([[User talk:Angr|''talk'']]) 21:55, 15 December 2014 (UTC) ::Yes, both spellings have been in use for over 400 years. The Greek ''{{m|grc|ἀπολογεῖσθαι}}'' could be a reason for using the ''s'' form. [[User:Dbfirs|''Dbfirs'']] 22:02, 16 December 2014 (UTC) :::Well, no; the earliest ''-ize'' words (such as {{m|en|baptize}}) came to English through the intermediaries of Latin and French, so a Greek middle infinitive is unlikely to have had any influence. I'm pretty sure the ''-ise'' variant was taken over from French {{m|fr|-iser}} while the ''-ize'' variant came straight from Latin {{m|la|-izō}}. —[[User:Angr|Aɴɢʀ]] ([[User talk:Angr|''talk'']]) 22:20, 16 December 2014 (UTC) ::::Thanks for the correction, and I agree with your view of the derivation, but why, then, do we have this insistence on going back to Greek forms? [[User:Dbfirs|''Dbfirs'']] 20:29, 17 December 2014 (UTC) :::::Who knows? I could equally ask why we have this insistence on using French spellings. —[[User:Angr|Aɴɢʀ]] ([[User talk:Angr|''talk'']]) 21:33, 17 December 2014 (UTC) {{archive-bottom}} ==pronunciation== In [[w:Vertigo (film)|the 1958 film ''Vertigo'']], Scottie Ferguson pronounces ''apologize'' with a /ɡ/. (About 56 minutes in, standing outside his apartment building.)​—[[User:Msh210|msh210]]℠ ([[user talk:Msh210|talk]]) 21:34, 4 April 2021 (UTC)

I count four syllables. [[User:John Cross|John Cross]] ([[User talk:John Cross|talk]]) 06:40, 3 June 2020 (UTC)
:Maybe some combine the the last two into "yum". I <s>see</s>hear their point. [[User:DCDuring|DCDuring]] ([[User talk:DCDuring|talk]]) 15:06, 3 June 2020 (UTC)
